summary: Describes additional attributes for carrying authentication, authorization and accounting information between a Network Access Server and a shared server using RADIUS, building on RFC 2865 and RFC 2866. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: This adds new items to the form that a door guard and a central list use to talk, covering things the original form left out.

questions: what is the radius eap-message attribute
subtitle: New RADIUS attributes for interim accounting, Apple Remote Access, and carrying EAP through a RADIUS server.

tldr.problem: RADIUS as defined in RFC 2865 and RFC 2866 had no standard way to carry interim accounting updates, to authenticate Apple Remote Access (ARAP) users, or to pass EAP authentication exchanges between a dial-in server and a RADIUS server.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines new attributes (types 52 to 88 in the ranges it lists), including Acct-Interim-Interval, the ARAP set, EAP-Message and Message-Authenticator. EAP packets travel inside EAP-Message attributes, and an HMAC-MD5 Message-Authenticator protects them.
tldr.outcome: The attributes were described as having little field experience and to be considered experimental. The memo is Informational and has since been updated by RFC 3579 and RFC 5080.

facts.label: Acct-Interim-Interval
facts.value: Type 85; MUST NOT be below 60 seconds

today: RFC 2869 is an Informational memo and has been updated by RFC 3579 and RFC 5080. It was not obsoleted by another RFC according to the metadata.

sections.title: Why Extend RADIUS
sections.content:
RFC 2865 describes the RADIUS protocol and RFC 2866 describes accounting with it. This memo suggests several additional attributes for useful functions. The RFC says they do not have extensive field experience yet and should be considered experimental.

All attributes are variable-length Type-Length-Value tuples, so new attribute values can be added without disturbing existing implementations. Operation, packet format and packet types are identical to those in RFC 2865 and RFC 2866.

One rule applies throughout: a NAS that does not implement a service MUST NOT implement the RADIUS attributes for that service, and it MUST treat an access-request for an unavailable service as an access-reject.
sections.eli5: The first rulebook for the door guard and the guest list was good but missing a few things. This note adds new, optional items without breaking the old ones.

sections.title: Interim Accounting Updates
sections.content:
To receive interim accounting messages for a user, the RADIUS server includes the Acct-Interim-Interval attribute in the Access-Accept. It gives the interval in seconds between interim messages. A value configured locally on the NAS MUST override the value in an Access-Accept.

This does not break backward interoperability: a server that does not support the extension simply does not add the attribute, and a NAS that does not support it ignores the attribute.

All information in an interim message is cumulative, so the packet count is the total since the session began. An interim record (Acct-Status-Type = Interim-Update (3)) is expected to carry the attributes of an Accounting Stop message except Acct-Term-Cause. Because of that, a NAS MUST keep only a single generation of an interim message per session in its retransmission queue. A NAS MAY add a random delay between sessions so that all updates are not sent at once.
sections.eli5: Like a teacher asking the bus driver to radio in every so often. Each radio call gives the whole total so far, not just the news since the last call.

sections.title: Apple Remote Access (ARAP) Support
sections.content:
The Apple Remote Access Protocol (ARAP) carries AppleTalk traffic over point-to-point links. Before this memo, ARAP connections on multi-protocol NAS devices were often not authenticated with RADIUS, or each vendor made its own solution. The memo adds a small set of ARAP attributes and assumes the RADIUS server can do DES encryption, in keeping with the goal of a smart server and a simple NAS.

ARAP authenticates in two phases. The first is a two-way DES random-number exchange using the user's password as the key. The second is optional and uses Apple's Add-In Security Modules, which the memo reduces to simple challenge and response cycles.

In the Access-Request, the NAS sends the user name (up to 31 characters), a Framed-Protocol of 3 (ARAP) and ARAP-Password. This 16-octet value carries the dial-in user's challenge to the NAS (high-order 8 octets) and the user's response to the NAS challenge (low-order 8 octets). On success the server returns Access-Accept with ARAP-Challenge-Response and ARAP-Features. On failure it returns Access-Reject, optionally with Password-Retry.

The memo does not address user-initiated password changes or out-of-band messages.
sections.eli5: Two people prove they both know a secret word by scrambling random numbers with it and checking each other's answers. The new boxes carry those scrambled numbers between the guard and the guest list.

sections.title: Carrying EAP Through RADIUS
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is a PPP extension that supports additional authentication methods. Two new attributes make it work over RADIUS: EAP-Message wraps EAP packets, and Message-Authenticator protects them. The NAS never needs to understand the EAP packets it forwards.

After EAP is negotiated, the NAS normally sends an EAP-Request/Identity to the peer, then forwards the reply in an Access-Request. To let EAP-unaware proxies forward the request, the NAS MUST copy the identity into the User-Name attribute. If no identity request is sent, the NAS can send an EAP-Message of length 2 with no data to signal EAP-Start, though that is not compatible with RFC 2865 and is hard to use with proxies.

A server that supports EAP MUST answer with an Access-Challenge carrying an EAP-Message; one that does not MUST answer Access-Reject. The conversation continues until an Access-Accept (with EAP-Success) or Access-Reject arrives. An Access-Reject MUST make the NAS send an LCP Terminate Request.

The NAS handles retransmission to the peer. The server can supply Session-Timeout and Password-Retry in an Access-Challenge, for example to give a token-card user more time, and the NAS can pass Framed-MTU so the server can size EAP packets. The memo also recommends RADIUS-encapsulated EAP between a RADIUS server and a backend security server.
sections.eli5: The guard passes sealed envelopes between the visitor and the guest list without opening them, and stamps each one so nobody can swap it on the way.

sections.title: The New Attributes
sections.content:
The memo defines these attribute types: Acct-Input-Gigawords (52), Acct-Output-Gigawords (53), Event-Timestamp (55), ARAP-Password (70), ARAP-Features (71), ARAP-Zone-Access (72), ARAP-Security (73), ARAP-Security-Data (74), Password-Retry (75), Prompt (76), Connect-Info (77), Configuration-Token (78), EAP-Message (79), Message-Authenticator (80), ARAP-Challenge-Response (84), Acct-Interim-Interval (85), NAS-Port-Id (87) and Framed-Pool (88).

The Gigawords attributes count how many times the 32-bit octet counters wrapped around 2^32. Acct-Interim-Interval MUST NOT be smaller than 60 seconds and SHOULD NOT be smaller than 600. Message-Authenticator is 18 octets long and is an HMAC-MD5 over the whole packet using the shared secret as the key, computed with the attribute value treated as sixteen zero octets. Multiple EAP-Message attributes are concatenated so EAP packets longer than 253 octets can be sent.

An Access-Request carrying a User-Password, CHAP-Password, ARAP-Password or EAP-Message MUST NOT contain more than one of those four types. Any packet with an EAP-Message MUST also contain a Message-Authenticator.
sections.eli5: This is the list of new boxes on the form, each with a number so everyone knows which is which.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Apart from Message-Authenticator and EAP-Message, the attributes add no security considerations beyond RFC 2865. The Message-Authenticator is needed because requests with CHAP-Password or EAP-Message have no User-Password to establish the identity of the NAS. The RFC says it thwarts a rogue NAS making online dictionary attacks, but gives no protection against offline attacks on captured CHAP exchanges, and that IP Security will eventually make it unnecessary, so it is an interim measure.

For EAP, the memo discusses several risks. If the EAP server and the PPP authenticator are separate machines, mutual authentication is between the peer and the EAP server, so the peer cannot validate the NAS, and the session key needs a transport mechanism outside the memo's scope. Because RADIUS has no encryption and its integrity protection is weaker than some EAP methods, all EAP/RADIUS packets MUST use Message-Authenticator. Shared secrets give no end-to-end security across proxies, separate user databases are a weakness, and negotiation attacks can push a user to weaker methods. The defence is per-connection policy at the peer and per-user policy at the server, and a peer that expects EAP MUST NOT negotiate CHAP or PAP.
sections.eli5: Without a seal on the envelopes, a sneaky helper in the middle could swap them. The seal, plus a rule to never accept a weaker lock, keeps the secret handshake safe.

items.label: Default zone only
items.desc: Only allow access to the default zone.

items.label: Inclusive filter
items.desc: Use the zone filter inclusively; a Filter-Id must be present.

items.label: Exclusive filter
items.desc: Use the zone filter exclusively; a Filter-Id must be present.
